claim: Children often do not vary one thing at a time when the problem is sparse, and some adults never fully grasp control of variables. At ages 7-13 the share of single-switch first tests ranged from 39% to 79% depending on age and sparsity (N=104): younger children chose single-switch tests most often (62.5% sparse, 79.3% dense), older children less often (39.3% sparse, 60.9% dense).
agent_test: Run the agent on switch-box style tasks; log the share of single-change tests with no prompt.
audit_note: Bramley data show younger children chose single-switch first tests most often (62.5% sparse, 79.3% dense); 'do not spontaneously vary one thing at a time' is not what the 39-79% range shows, and Peteranderl only says some adults do not fully grasp CVS, not many.
claim_before_audit: Children and many adults do not spontaneously vary one thing at a time. At ages 7-13 the first-test share of single-switch tests ranged from 39% to 79% depending on age and sparsity (N=104).

claim: Whether one change per test is the best test depends on causal sparsity. With few true causes among many candidates, testing about half at once (split-half) is the ideal strategy (expected return about 1.90 euro in the sparse switch-box condition), whereas in the dense condition testing one switch at a time is the only effective strategy (about 1.25 euro); so 'one change per test' is not universally optimal. Bramley et al. (N=104): first test used several switches in 60.7% of older children on sparse boxes vs 39.1% on dense. LLM agents show a related boundary: with AND (joint-cause) rules models struggle and improve when they sample and eliminate hypotheses (GX-Chen 2025); human adults in conjunctive worlds shift from 1-object to 2-object tests (Samiei 2026), and strong models rely mainly on one- or two-object interventions.
agent_test: Compare strict one-change vs split-half tests on sparse and dense synthetic causal tasks at equal test budget. S4 should say one change when many causes are plausible, grouped tests when few are expected.
audit_note: The 1.90 (split-half, sparse) vs 1.25 (one-at-a-time, dense) figures come from different conditions so they do not show split-half beating one-at-a-time; Samiei reports the 1-to-2-object shift for human adults, while strong models rely on sparse one- or two-object interventions.
claim_before_audit: Whether one change per test is the best test depends on causal sparsity. With few true causes among many candidates, testing about half at once beats one at a time (expected return about 1.90 vs 1.25 one-at-a-time in the dense case). So 'one change per test' is not universally optimal. Bramley et al. (N=104): first test used several switches in 60.7% of older children on sparse boxes vs 39.1% on dense. LLM agents show the same boundary: with AND (joint-cause) rules, one-object tests cannot decide, and models fail unless they sample and eliminate hypotheses (GX-Chen 2025); successful adults and strong models move from 1-object to 2-object tests in conjunctive worlds (Samiei 2026).

claim: CVS can be taught: mean g=0.61 over 72 interventions (second-hand via Peteranderl). It works best when the teacher explains and the child also designs experiments (72% vs 65% vs 57%, Freer Study 1). Physical and virtual materials work equally (Triona & Klahr).
agent_test: Add a short worked CVS rule plus one designed example to S4; compare to plain at equal tokens.

claim: Starting from confounded designs and repairing them beats showing only clean designs (84% vs 73% in high-achieving schools, 69% vs 56% in low-achieving, immediate). Four variables beat two as teaching material.
agent_test: Give the agent a confounded test to fix before real testing; measure the confounded-test rate afterwards.

claim: Direct instruction gets more children to master CVS than pure discovery in the short run (Klahr & Nigam N=112; Strand-Cary & Klahr N=72 repeated it at grades 3-5; Lorch classroom trial of 800+ children: lecture plus experiments > lecture > experiments). The headline 77% vs 23% is still NOT verified. Long-run and transfer qualifications: Dean & Kuhn (3 groups of 15) found direct instruction neither necessary nor sufficient for lasting skill; an invent-then-tell vs tell-then-practice study (N=101) found a tie; Kaiser found no benefit of self-generation.
agent_test: State the one-change rule in S4 text and also repeat the check at every test; compare against no rule and against rule stated once.

claim: Understanding that evidence can be indeterminate and that confounding blocks inference are precursors of later CVS (together 39% of variance, N=170). Preschoolers (N=57) show the pieces separately and unrelated.
agent_test: Check whether the agent says 'this result cannot tell which change did it' when two things changed.

claim: Choosing a good test and drawing the right inference from the result are separate skills. Older children used multi-switch tests and got 17/19 right; younger children who did got 3/7. Preschool recognition of confounds does not predict controlled choice. Correction from re-reading Moeller et al.: preschoolers showed some recognition of confounded evidence and above-chance controlled-test choice in some tasks, but the two were unrelated; so the 'opposite dissociation' with Bramley is mostly a difference in task and measure, not a clean reversal.
agent_test: Score test design and inference-from-result separately in agent traces.

claim: Reading comprehension and maths skill predicted the pretest-posttest gain in experimenting (CVS) in fifth-graders (Schlatter 2020, N=138, gains uneven across components: hypothesis-evidence coordination and drawing conclusions did not gain significantly). Separately, theory of mind at age 4 predicted scientific reasoning at 5.5 and 7.5, controlling for executive function and language, which also related to scientific reasoning (Sobel 2026).
agent_test: Context only; no agent mechanism.
audit_note: Reading and maths predicting CVS (experimenting) gain scores is shown by Schlatter; Sobel shows theory of mind (and, as a related factor, executive function) relating to scientific reasoning in ages 4-7.5, not CVS gains specifically.
claim_before_audit: Reading and maths skill, theory of mind and executive function predict CVS gains and later scientific reasoning in children. Gains are uneven across components.

claim: People hold theory-confirming strategies and change several variables at once in multivariable systems. In MicroDYN (N=4371) users who apply vary-one-thing knowingly solve best, then unaware VOTAT users, then others.
agent_test: Compare forced-VOTAT vs free test choice on MicroDYN-style tasks for an LLM. Only b15 was opened; a20 and b16 are unread.

claim: LLMs show confirmation bias in rule discovery: they propose tests that fit their current hypothesis, and more positive tests means lower success (Spearman -0.779 across 12 models in FalsifyBench; same sign in an independent 11-model study).
agent_test: Add an S4 rule: include at least one test expected to fail under the current hypothesis. Measure success at equal tokens.

claim: Counterexample-seeking prompts raise LLM rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average over 11 LLMs, but help little for small non-thinking models (Qwen3-8B 0.06 to 0.06). Single study, prompt effect not replicated. Appendix tables: non-thinking instruct models, baseline / opposites prompt: Qwen3-8B 0.06/0.06, 14B 0.23/0.29, 32B 0.33/0.36, Llama-3.3-70B 0.21/0.38; the Dual-Goal prompt lowered 14B and 32B (0.13, 0.10). Thinking models gain more (for example Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.60) at about 40% more tokens per turn. No test on a pretrained base model; no independent replication.
agent_test: Replicate the opposites prompt on our base model for 2-4-6 and a CVS task at equal tokens.

claim: Reasoning models test negatively and falsify far more than instruction-tuned models (positive-test share 27% for GPT-5.2-Chat vs 66-82% for instruction-tuned; rho(bias, falsification) = -0.937).
agent_test: Measure the positive-test share of our agent with and without a reasoning budget.
audit_note: Numbers (27% vs 66-82%, rho -0.937) come from FalsifyBench alone; Jhaveri only supports the qualitative direction (reasoning-trace models show lower bias).

claim: Humans who choose their own tests do well on conjunctive rules (0.69); those who propose tests without seeing outcomes do worst (0.12). LLMs given the same actions explore less efficiently than humans. The 'proposer' group saw outcomes of another person's tests, not outcomes of its own written batch, so the result supports 'choose the next test after seeing the last outcome' but does not directly test batched plans. In conjunctive worlds successful agents shifted from 1-object to 2-object tests.
agent_test: Check that the agent sees each test outcome before proposing the next; check whether batching proposals hurts.

claim: LLM agents are weak at end-to-end experimentation. DiscoveryWorld completion is 0.38 (easy) to 0.08-0.18 (challenge) vs humans 0.66; ScienceWorld best 0.17; MLAgentBench 37.5%; ScienceAgentBench 32.4%. No agent solved several tasks.
agent_test: Use as difficulty baseline; none of these is a CVS test.
audit_note: ScienceWorld 0.17 is the best model overall (DRRN, an RL agent, not an LLM agent); ScienceAgentBench 32.4% excludes o1-preview which reached 42.2% at over 10x cost.

claim: An explicit hypothesis step helps knowledge on easy DiscoveryWorld tasks but hurts completion on challenge tasks (0.08 vs 0.18 for ReAct).
agent_test: Test whether an explicit hypothesis step pays for itself at equal tokens on hard tasks.

claim: More variables break agents: on proteomics measurement ReAct scored 0.00 on both 2-variable and 5-variable versions, and Plan+Execute 0.00 on 5 variables (5 seeds).
agent_test: Scale the number of candidate causes in a synthetic task and chart accuracy.

claim: A Bayesian modelling tool or prior information does not reliably help LLM experiment design (BoxingGym). A written explanation from an experimenter helps a novice less than running the experiments.
agent_test: Test whether passing written lessons from past tests helps less than re-running the check.

claim: A controlled-experiment agent with a requirement-analysis step improved expert-rated correctness (4.1 vs under 3.0) and simulator-call precision (94% vs 65% without the step) in one pharma simulator.
agent_test: Narrow domain; test an S4 pre-check asking what comparison is needed before calling the check.

claim: No LLM study was found that tests control-of-variables or confounded-evidence judgement with developmental items. The nearest are 2-4-6 games, ACED, BoxingGym and DiscoveryWorld, none framed as CVS. A second search (ERIC, Europe PMC, PubMed, citation lists) also found none for LLM plus MicroDYN or VOTAT; arXiv search itself was rate-limited, so recent preprints could be missed.
agent_test: Build a small CVS item set (ramps, switch box) and run the agent. This is the main missing measurement.
audit_note: Absence claim cannot be proven; no CVS framing found in text of DiscoveryWorld, ScienceWorld, GX-Chen or Samiei, and one extra search found none.

claim: Added scaffolds that ask which variables could have caused the outcome improved far transfer and removed dependence on pretest (88% vs 83% mastery; N=33). Small sample.
agent_test: Prompt the agent to list candidate causes before testing and compare.

claim: Advanced students often accept a causal claim from correlational evidence (66% found a correlational study convincing, N=97 completers). A short example-based lesson reduced the error.
agent_test: Probe the agent with correlational vs interventional evidence items.

claim: LLM agents given one object per step show a disjunctive bias: they solve OR rules and fail on AND rules, more so with 8 objects than 4, while an information-gain oracle solves both. More reasoning effort in o-mini models made AND exploration worse. Sampling and eliminating many hypotheses removed the gap.
agent_test: Run a switch-box item set with AND and OR rules; compare 'one change per test' alone vs 'list candidate causes, then pick the test that splits them'.

claim: Choosing the next test after seeing the previous outcome matters. Adults who only proposed tests and saw other people's outcomes scored 0.12 on object identification in conjunctive worlds vs 0.69 for active choosers. LLMs do not reliably gain from choosing their own tests.
agent_test: Compare a sequential loop (choose, run, update) against a pre-written batch of tests at equal tokens.

claim: Segmenting a multivariable task so only one variable is open at a time works as well as direct instruction for children (22 vs 23 vs 22 per group), and a one-line instruction to focus on a single factor raised controlled comparison in low-achieving sixth graders. Both are the mechanical form of S4.
agent_test: Test a one-line 'focus on one factor' wording against a long CVS rule at equal tokens.

claim: CVS has two halves that are taught by different things: lecture improves holding irrelevant variables constant, hands-on experimenting improves varying the focal variable (Lorch 2010, 800+ children). Planning controlled tests and spotting confounded ones respond to training; identifying and interpreting controlled tests develop without it (N=618).
agent_test: Check both halves in S4: 'is exactly one thing different?' and 'did I vary the thing I care about?'.
audit_note: Lorch 2010 abstract gives n=797 (WWC review 848), not strictly 800+; the N=618 study (J Educ Psychol 2023, ETH record) is not the cited ERIC EJ1039461 page (Lazonder and Egberink 2014, n=67), so that half was confirmed only through a search snippet.

claim: Showing invalid (confounded) designs to explain CVS beat showing only valid ones on far transfer (n=1,069); high guidance beat low guidance (N=57); invent-then-tell tied with tell-then-practice (N=101).
agent_test: Add one worked confounded example to S4 and measure transfer to new item types.

claim: LLMs propose and revise hypotheses well but pick experiments poorly: a plain ReAct agent scored 4.60 of 8 on a Zendo-style game, average humans 5.26, and an information-gain scaffold 6.55. Evidence-ledger studies list the same agent failures (wrong test, lost evidence, no stopping).
agent_test: Add a step that scores candidate tests by how many remaining hypotheses they split.

claim: Kuhn's microgenetic work (1995: 17 adults and 15 fourth graders) found strategies mixed within a person and over time, with a published critique that stages were partly produced by the experimenter's questions. Later work shows multivariable integration stays hard for years. No percentages were read, and no formal failed replication was found.
agent_test: Log whether the agent keeps a refuted hypothesis across a multi-session task.

claim: The Jhaveri 42% to 56% opposites effect has no independent replication. FalsifyBench (a second lab) tests no prompts and one rule-discovery task, but agrees that reasoning models test negatively more and succeed more than instruction-tuned ones.
agent_test: Replicate on a held-out rule family and one non-rule task.
